request.system:
You assist an automated astronomer who infers how a body moves from angles-only sky observations (ecliptic longitude/latitude seen from an observer whose orbit is known). Jan, the fitting engine, fits candidate model families by least squares and compares them by Bayesian evidence. You see numerical summaries of the current best fit and its residuals, and you propose the next candidates to fit.

A candidate is either a registered family (by exact name) or a new central force law: the radial acceleration f(r) in AU/day^2 (negative = attractive) as an expression in r (heliocentric distance, AU), GM (the Sun's, 2.959e-4 AU^3/day^2, fixed) and parameters you declare with bounds and an initial value. Allowed in expressions: numbers, + - * / **, parentheses, exp, log, sqrt, tanh, pi, r, GM and your parameter names (lowercase, letters/digits/underscore). Prefer the simplest law that explains the residual structure; a new parameter must buy a clear improvement. Reply "stop": true when the residuals are consistent with noise or further candidates are unlikely to help.

parsed.analysis:
The free power law (n≈1.75, C≈0.77·GM) is clearly the best so far. Its retrograde apsidal motion (−39°/orbit) matches what a power law with n=1.75 predicts. However, the residuals are not pure noise. The periodogram has a dominant peak at 343 d, about twice the orbital frequency (P≈685 d). The time-binned mean east residuals reach 5–8σ, so a systematic misfit remains.

A key constraint is how strong and how steep the force is near r≈1.44 AU. The fit says the force there is weaker than Newton's, yet it falls off less steeply than 1/r². Adding any single term to an unchanged GM/r² cannot produce both effects at once. This explains why newton_plus_hooke, the inverse-cube correction and Yukawa all lost.

A softened (Plummer-like) mass distribution produces both effects naturally. Matching the fitted force and slope at r≈1.44 requires a softening length b≈0.43 AU and a mass parameter mu≈2.85e-4, which is very close to GM. So I propose:
- a one-parameter Plummer law with the Sun's GM fixed;
- the same law with free mu;
- a scaled-Newton-plus-Hooke law as an alternative that also allows a mass rescaling.

All three may also change the higher-harmonic shape of the orbit, which would address the 2×orbital-frequency residual.

proposals.rationale: Softened point mass with the Sun's GM fixed. At r≈1.44 AU, b≈0.43 AU reproduces both the effective index n≈1.75 and the reduced force strength. Only one parameter, versus two for the power law.
Same softened law with free mass. It has the same parameter count as the power law but a different higher-order radial shape, which could absorb the residual at twice the orbital frequency.
Newton plus Hooke failed because GM was fixed. Freeing the mass lets the law give a weaker force with n<2, with curvature different from a pure power law.
